transcript:
Header: 2026-02-17 16:00 UTC | Duration: 44m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Douglas (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (Ivory CTO), Sofia Martinez (ML Eng), Ravi Patel (Product), Janelle (Finance)
---
Summary: quick optimize walkthrough of batching and KV/prefix caching economics. Focus on practical numbers for Ivory's telemetry and the tradeoffs if they tune for lower cost vs tighter latency SLO.
---
00:00 - Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda - we'll run through the console optimize tab, show batching knobs, prefix (kv) cache assumptions, and then plug in a small cost model using a sample traffic shape.
00:14 - Ethan Park: Great thanks, Maya. high level, our users have conversational sessions, avg request length around 180 tokens, responses 220 tokens, sessions often 6-8 turns. latency at 500ms p90 is our goal, and we want to see how much Redwood can save vs our current self-hosted baseline.
00:30 - Liam Douglas: ok that helps. when we say sessions of 6-8 turns that suggests lookahead / prefix caching can really help if the majority of tokens are prefixes or system prompts. quick question: are you already doing session affinity on your side?
00:46 - Sofia Martinez: yeah we sticky to sessions for now, but the distribution is spiky — peak hour concurrency hits are the pain. we can share some histograms.
01:02 - Maya Chen: perfect, please share. we'll model both sessionized prefetch and a TTL-based KV cache. in the console demo i want to show two scenarios: conservative latency-first batching and aggressive batching for cost savings.
01:18 - Liam Douglas: note: continuous batching reduces unit cost but increases tail latency variance. also cache hit rate assumptions are super sensitive — going from 30% to 60% hit changes token spend dramatically.
01:35 - Ravi Patel: can you quantify "dramatically" in the model? CFO wants numbers we can show.
:01:44 - Priya Nair: sure; in the sample sheet we'll show 3 cols — baseline no-cache, moderate cache (40% hit) and high cache (65% hit). we'll estimate tokens served and then compute per-day cost given your token rates.
02:02 - Ethan Park: what's the realistic hit for a commerce/analytics chat? our prompts include dynamic data, so prefixes change some per user.
02:16 - Liam Douglas: that's where prefix-trimming plus small session KV works — keep system + few-turn prefixes in cache with a short TTL (e.g., 10-30m) and rely on lookahead to populate KV for active users. if your dynamic tokens are only in the last 20 tokens, hit rates can still be 45%+.
02:37 - Sofia Martinez: hmm ok. show us the TTL tradeoffs.
02:41 - Maya Chen: switching to the console screen share now — (screen noise) opening the Optimize tab > Cost Simulator.
03:05 - [screen commentary] Maya Chen: here is the traffic input panel — paste your request size distribution. i'll paste a synthetic trace we used in similar pilots: median request tokens 180, median response 220, session length 7, concurrency 1,200 peak.
03:28 - Liam Douglas: watch the batch size slider — default continuous batching uses a small time-window and will batch up to N requests depending on concurrency and latency target. if you move aggressiveness to high, we coalesce more requests into a single GPU run, lowering per-token price, but p95 latency can climb ~50-120ms depending on sequence lengths.
03:54 - Ethan Park: how do we ensure the 500ms p90 holds?
04:00 - Priya Nair: you set a latency SLO in the routing policy. we simulate and show expected p50/p90/p95 against the batch config. you can also pin to a lower-capacity host and use fallback routing to keep p90 tighter at a cost.
04:18 - Ravi Patel: show me an example with numeric outputs please.
04:22 - Maya Chen: ok running scenario A: latency-first, batch aggressiveness low. Model: open-model-7b-equivalent, tokens/day 85M (derived from your avg). console estimate: daily cost $1,800 ; p90 latency 420ms ; batch utilization 1.3x.
04:48 - Sophia (sic) Martinez (mis-transcribed): wait 85M seems low, are you counting both request+response tokens?
04:55 - Liam Douglas: good catch — yes that is total tokens (request + response). we'll put the breakdown in the spreadsheet.
05:06 - Maya Chen: scenario B: cost-first, batch high, prefix-KV enabled with 45% hit assumption and 20m TTL. same traffic shape yields daily cost $980, p90 latency 560ms, batch utilization 2.8x. that's ~45% cost savings vs scenario A in the model.
05:28 - Ethan Park: 560ms p90 is borderline. our customer delight team wants <500ms for 80% of queries. is there a hybrid?
05:35 - Priya Nair: yes hybrid routing: route 60% of requests (critical paths) to latency-first path and 40% to cost-first. console lets you configure route weights and auto-fallback on capacity. the simulated blended cost: $1,420/day, blended p90 ~480ms, and effective cache hit is slightly lower because we route active sessions differently.
06:02 - Ravi Patel: nice. what about TTL churn — will frequent TTL evictions kill the hit rate?
06:09 - Liam Douglas: TTL needs to be chosen with session characteristics. a 20m TTL for users with ~10 minute inter-turn time is decent. eviction churn increases backend KV read load which is small relative to token costs but important for tail latencies.
06:25 - Janelle (Finance): can you show a sensitivity table? like cost vs hit rate?
06:30 - Maya Chen: yes i have that in the sheet. popping it up: columns for 20%, 35%, 50%, 65% hit. at 20% hit we see only 12% savings; at 50% hit we get ~40-50% savings. the curve is non-linear because each cached token prevents both request compute and response generation in many cases.
06:52 - Sofia Martinez: what about warm-start / lookahead for new sessions?
07:00 - Liam Douglas: lookahead prefetching on session start can prime the KV with expected next prompts. it works best when flows are templated. downside: extra token cost on prefetch that may not be used; so we model tradeoff in console by showing expected prefetch hit rate vs wasted token spend.
07:24 - Ethan Park: curious — can we limit prefetch to only verified returning users? we have a cookie and user id.
07:30 - Priya Nair: yes you can gate prefetch by session signals and user flags. that reduces wasted prefetch spend and increases effective hit rate.
07:38 - Maya Chen: switching to the throughput simulator — this is where Liam will run a quick micro-sim with their sample trace. Liam, take it away.
07:46 - Liam Douglas: starting the sim; this will approximate continuous batching behavior on a single GPU pool of 4k tokens/s capability (sim numbers for demo). initial run with no cache: peak throughput 3,100 qps-equivalent, average batch size 1.4, cost est $1,800/day.
08:10 - [typing sounds]
08:21 - Liam Douglas: enabling KV cache with 45% hit, TTL 20m: throughput requirement drops ~28% due to fewer tokens generated, batch size increases to 2.7 on average because more short requests are coalesced, cost est $1,020/day.
08:42 - Ethan Park: those numbers look promising. are the sim assumptions conservative? i.e., real runtime maybe slightly different?
08:50 - Liam Douglas: sims are conservative for inference variance and include extra padding for cache misses; actual runtime in a pilot can vary +/- 10-20%. we recommend an on-prem-ish pilot for full verification.
09:03 - Ravi Patel: what about quantized models or variants; can we switch to an 8-bit variant to save cost?
09:11 - Priya Nair: yes we support recommended quantization profiles. the console will show model variant comparisons; lower-precision variants reduce token cost but change latency profile. we usually surface perf profiles for each model.
09:24 - Maya Chen: moving to objections — Ethan raised data residency and encryption earlier. quick note: for Dedicated or Private deployments we can meet stricter KMS/HSM and VPC controls. for hosted, we have SOC2 controls and audit logs.
09:45 - Ethan Park: we need SOC2 + evidence of KMS integration for legal. also SAML SSO for RBAC.
09:52 - Maya Chen: we will share the security pack. action item for Maya.
10:00 - Sofia Martinez: ok back to costing, can you attach the CSV with the sim runs? that will help our finance folks.
10:06 - Maya Chen: yes, will attach.
10:10 - [long silence / screen scroll]
10:25 - Lily (mispelled) asked about eviction policy — sorry that was Janelle?
10:30 - Liam Douglas: eviction policy — LRU is default for the KV; you can tune by frequency and by weight (system prompts pinned). also we expose metrics for cache hit by prefix type.
10:48 - Ravi Patel: what's the operational complexity? how much change to our app?
10:54 - Maya Chen: minimal; we provide a small SDK snippet to push session keys and prefix updates to the KV. most teams instrument a middleware to handle sessionization. estimated dev effort: 2-3 engineer-weeks for a basic pilot integration.
11:12 - Ethan Park: ok that's doable. our Q is pilot sizing — what's a realistic pilot footprint?
11:18 - Priya Nair: we recommend a 2-week pilot at 5-10% traffic routed to Redwood with dedicated capacity of 2-4 GPUs depending on concurrency. we'll size it once we have your trace.
11:32 - Maya Chen: now going to the risk table in the sheet — row 1: cache miss spikes; mitigations: fallback routing + increased autoscaling. row 2: prefix churn — mitigations: lower TTL + gated prefetch. row 3: cold user behavior — mitigations: no prefetch for cold users.
11:55 - Sofia Martinez: are there any vendor lock-in concerns if we adopt Redwood's KV API?
12:02 - Liam Douglas: KV API is simple — you can export session keys and data; we don't require proprietary encoding. also the console's recommendations can be ported to other runtimes if you wanted to self-host later.
12:18 - Ethan Park: finance question: how do we book committed cost vs variable?
12:23 - Maya Chen: Hosted is usage-based; Dedicated offers reserved capacity commitments that reduce unit price. we can show a break-even analysis in the spreadsheet for reserved vs usage at your projected volume.
12:35 - Ravi Patel: can you run the reserved capacity breakeven with our traffic?
12:39 - Maya Chen: yes, if you share the trace. we'll include it in the follow-up.
12:44 - [background chatter]
12:55 - Priya Nair: quick FYI — token accounting in the console includes padding allowances we call "execution overhead" which covers KV fetch overhead and some model padding; it's adjustable.
13:08 - Ethan Park: what about multi-region routing? some of our users are APAC.
13:14 - Priya Nair: console supports region-based policies; you can route APAC into nearest region and fallback to another region if capacity scarce. this affects cost and latency; the sim can model multi-region splits.
13:29 - Janelle: is there any compliance concern for the KV storing PII? we might have user names in prompts.
13:36 - Maya Chen: by default we recommend redaction; for private deployments you can use customer-managed KMS and configure retention TTLs; also see our PII handling guide in the security pack.
13:52 - Ethan Park: good. last set of technical clarifications before we wrap: 1) how is batching affected by streaming responses? 2) how do we measure cache hit for partial prefixes?
14:04 - Liam Douglas: 1) streaming can begin as soon as the model produces tokens, but batching decisions are made before generation; with streaming we may still batch, but initial latency may be marginally higher. 2) partial prefix hits are tracked as a hit fractioned by token overlap; console exposes both "prefix key hit" and "token-saved estimate" metrics.
14:30 - Maya Chen: ok quick recap: share trace + sample metrics (Ethan), Redwood sends full cost workbook + console recording (Maya), Redwood runs throughput sim on the trace and posts numbers (Liam). agreed follow-up: week of 2026-02-23 to review sim.
14:50 - Ethan Park: sounds good. thank you all.
15:00 - [meeting ends]
---
